claim_atom: In the original Dryad deposit (v1, 2020), the body-size column SL is misaligned to Fish.ID: for Fish.ID 5 the four rows (its four behavioural observations) carry DIFFERENT SL values (D2=21.21, D3=20.22, D4=22.66, D5=21.96 mm), which is impossible because standard length (SL) is a single per-individual body-size measurement that cannot change across the four repeated behavioural trials of the same fish. 78 of 94 fish show the same within-individual SL variation. The corrected 2026 deposit makes the error explicit by carrying two columns, 'Bad.SL' (the original mis-assigned values, e.g. ID=1 row = 21.08/20.48/22.58/22.18) and 'Correct.SL' (constant per fish, e.g. 23.66 for all four rows of ID=1). The authors acknowledged on PubPeer that the Dryad body-size/SL data were misaligned to Fish ID and updated the deposited data and the paper.

paper_title: Human HDAC6 senses valine abundancy to regulate DNA damage
claim_atom: In Source Data Fig. 4c, the shHDAC6 'VR (24 h)' column (E5:E39) equals the shHDAC6 'VR (0 h)' column (D5:D39) minus exactly 0.30 percentage points for all 35 fields of view, byte-for-byte (e.g. E5 0.15 = D5 0.45 - 0.30; E24 3.04 = D24 3.34 - 0.30). The two columns are the γH2AX-positive-cell percentages of two independent conditions (0 h vs 24 h of valine restriction), each derived from counts of anywhere between 100 and 10,000 cells per field with no row-by-row correspondence in cell totals. A fixed 0.30-point offset holding across all 35 independent fields cannot arise from genuine per-field counting and is a fabrication signature (PubPeer commenter Van Kampen estimates such cross-column arithmetic identities to be astronomically improbable). The authors' 'Gen5 counting + positive/total x100' explanation accounts only for the decimal granularity of a single value, not for the exact 0.30 offset between two independent series; Tongji University's 2026-05-06 investigation ruled that the cell counts in the gamma-H2AX figures were not objectively performed, constituting academic misconduct.

claim_atom: PubPeer comment #4 flagged that some Fig. 4c columns have '4' in the second decimal place (e.g. shHDAC6 D24 = 3.34) while adjacent columns have '5' (e.g. shTET2 F24 = 3.15), implying a suspicious pattern. Considered in isolation, this terminal-digit heterogeneity is NOT by itself evidence of manipulation: a percentage computed as (gamma-H2AX-positive cells / total nuclei) x 100 is quantized by its per-condition denominator, so conditions counted over different cell totals legitimately produce different achievable terminal decimals. In the source data this is visible as column-dependent granularity (shNC column B is 35/35 multiples of 0.05 with tails 0/5; shHDAC6 columns D/E carry '...4' tails), exactly what different denominators predict. This specific 'why do the terminal digits differ' signal is therefore consistent with the stated count/total computation and is a false-positive trap; it does NOT on its own establish fabrication, which is instead established by the exact cross-column offsets of claim_001.

claim_atom: In the Source Data for Extended Data Fig. 1a (hippocampal SLM), the 'Total SPP1 immunoreactivity per tile' column contains 15 tile-level rows for NLF drawn from only 9 mice: several mice contribute three tiles each that were counted as independent replicates (e.g. mouse NLF186 gives D28,D29,D30 = 21.696, 6.414, 28.463 — a >4-fold within-mouse spread). The corrected file itself adds a 'Per-mouse' column (F/G) that collapses these three tiles into a single per-mouse value G30 = 18.857667 ('NLF186 average (of datapoints 21.696; 6.414; 28.463)'). Treating the 15 tiles (and 16 WT tiles) as independent n inflates the degrees of freedom relative to the true unit of replication (the animal, n=9 NLF / n=10 WT), i.e. pseudoreplication that inflates the significance of the reported hippocampal SPP1 difference. This matches the PubPeer critique (15 NLF / 16 WT source points vs 8 plotted; p reported as 0.0499) and the pseudoreplication concern that the authors explicitly declined to correct.

claim_atom: The paper's headline claim for this panel is that SPP1 upregulation is region-specific — elevated in hippocampus but NOT in cerebellum. In the cerebellum half (Extended Data Fig. 1b), collapsing to the corrected per-mouse values shows no NLF elevation: a representative NLF cerebellar mouse G14 = 6.4735 is LOWER than a representative WT cerebellar mouse G16 = 7.67, and across the panel the NLF and WT per-mouse cerebellar means overlap (NLF ~= 8-10, WT ~= 9-11). Thus the 'no SPP1 upregulation in cerebellum' half of the region-specificity statement is direction-robust to per-mouse aggregation and is not affected by the pseudoreplication that inflates the hippocampal comparison. This is consistent with the authors' response that per-mouse re-analysis (e.g. Fig. 1b per-mouse P = 0.0043) does not overturn the qualitative regional finding.

claim_atom: Whether the hippocampal SPP1 elevation is actually statistically significant once analysed at the mouse level, and whether the paper's 'region-specific' wording is justified, both hinge on a region x genotype interaction test (the mouse NLF107 is measured in both regions: SLM D23 = 13.0715 vs CB D2 = 12.603333, and other mice similarly), which was never reported. Multiple commenters (and a Nature Neuroscience tutorial cited in the thread) note the paper compares two separate p-values on either side of 0.05 rather than testing the interaction, and never provides the per-mouse P value for ED Fig. 1a. The published Correction (s41593-025-02197-6) revised some statistics and source files but the corresponding author stated the pseudoreplication concern would NOT be addressed, and the region-specificity interaction remains untested in the public record. Adjudication of whether the hippocampus-vs-cerebellum region specificity holds is therefore pending.
